Dialogue 04: More people is not a higher percentage
Original fictional setting: During a fifteen-minute office-hour meeting, student Noor asks why a chart cannot show that Group B had the higher participation rate merely because more people participated. Group A has 40 participants out of 100 eligible people; Group B has 60 out of 200. Professor Evans uses the supplied figures to distinguish counts from rates. The meeting does not determine a grade or change an assessment deadline.
Professional roles: Noor / Professor Evans
Published dialogue (reference script, not my own performance):
Noor: I thought Group B performed better because sixty people participated, compared with forty in Group A. The feedback says to check the rate.
Professor Evans: Let us set a short meeting agenda: first distinguish the quantities, then use the two groups to check the idea.
Noor: I compared the number of people and did not look at how many people were eligible in each group.
Professor Evans: That identifies the learning bottleneck. You are using an absolute count to answer a question about a proportion.
Noor: Group A had one hundred eligible people, while Group B had two hundred, so the groups were not the same size.
Professor Evans: Exactly. The denominator tells us the whole against which the participant count is being compared.
Noor: Then forty is the part for Group A, and sixty is the part for Group B.
Professor Evans: Those are the numerator values. For A, forty out of one hundred gives forty percent.
Noor: For B, sixty out of two hundred gives thirty percent, even though sixty is the larger number of participants.
Professor Evans: Good. That is the worked example: B has the larger count, while A has the higher participation rate.
Noor: I can see why putting both raw counts on a chart does not by itself answer which group had the higher proportion.
Professor Evans: That is the purpose of normalization here. We compare each count with its own eligible population rather than treating the groups as equal in size.
Noor: Would it be accurate to say B had more participants but a lower share of its eligible population?
Professor Evans: Yes. That sentence separates the absolute count from the proportional measure and keeps both facts intact.
Noor: I initially thought the feedback meant sixty was the wrong number, but the number was right and my interpretation was wrong.
Professor Evans: That is a conceptual misunderstanding rather than a transcription error. Understanding the distinction will help with other unequal-size groups.
Noor: Can we check it once more without looking at the completed percentages, using the same supplied figures?
Professor Evans: Certainly. That retrieval practice will show whether you can reconstruct the reasoning instead of recognizing an answer that is already written.
Noor: A is forty percent and B is thirty percent. I will identify the eligible population whenever I report a participation rate.
Professor Evans: That completes the concept check. Use the distinction in your next practice, and bring any remaining specific question to a follow-up meeting.
Vocabulary in this exchange: meeting agenda: Agreed focus for a discussion. / worked example: Example showing the reasoning or steps of a solution. / conceptual misunderstanding: Incorrect understanding of an underlying idea. / numerator: Quantity above the fraction line, representing the counted part here. / denominator: Quantity below the fraction line, representing the eligible group here. / absolute count: Number of observed items or people without normalization.
END REFERENCE

Dialogue 05: Fluent wording is not the missing reasoning
Original fictional setting: Professor Malik and teaching assistant Elena use a fictional three-level evidence scale: 0 for no relevant evidence, 1 for relevant evidence without an explained link, and 2 for relevant evidence with an explained link. An anchor response contains a relevant quotation but no explanation of its connection. Elena gave 2 because the prose was fluent; Malik applied 1. Grades have not been released.
Professional roles: Elena / Professor Malik
Published dialogue (reference script, not my own performance):
Elena: I gave this response two points because it reads fluently and includes a relevant quotation. Your score is one.
Professor Malik: Let us return to the scoring guide. What distinguishes level one from level two on this evidence scale?
Elena: Level two requires the response to explain how the evidence supports the conclusion. This response leaves that connection unstated.
Professor Malik: Then our anchor response demonstrates level one, even though the prose is fluent.
Elena: I allowed the polished wording to influence my judgment about whether the reasoning was complete.
Professor Malik: That is criterion contamination. We need to keep the evidence dimension separate from any criterion assessing expression.
Elena: I can explain the one-point score as relevant quotation present, but the explanatory link is absent.
Professor Malik: That gives a clear scoring rationale that another grader can inspect and discuss.
Elena: Should we compare a second example where the link is partly implied? That seems more difficult than this clear case.
Professor Malik: Yes. A borderline response can expose where we interpret the descriptor differently, without rewriting the published standard.
Elena: We can score it independently first and then compare the passages each of us relied on.
Professor Malik: That supports grading calibration. The purpose is consistent judgment, not simply having the junior colleague copy a senior score.
Elena: I may have applied the same fluency shortcut to other papers in my batch, so correcting this one example is not enough.
Professor Malik: Then define a batch review under our assessment process and identify the work that needs checking.
Elena: The grades are still unreleased. I can keep the results from being published while we complete the agreed check.
Professor Malik: Maintain the release hold and make the reason clear to the teaching team, without exposing student work unnecessarily.
Elena: For the briefing, I will use the approved anonymized examples and show the criterion alongside the relevant passages.
Professor Malik: Good. That should improve inter-rater agreement by making our interpretation and evidence visible.
Elena: Once the review is complete, I will report what was checked and any changes made through the approved process.
Professor Malik: Then we can seek release approval. A calibration conversation is a useful step, but it is not the same as completing and authorizing the release.
Vocabulary in this exchange: grading calibration: Process of aligning application of assessment standards. / anchor response: Selected example used to illustrate a scoring standard. / scoring guide: Instructions explaining how to assign marks. / inter-rater agreement: Degree of consistency between assessors. / borderline response: Work near the boundary between performance levels. / criterion contamination: Influence of an unrelated feature on a criterion judgment.
END REFERENCE

Dialogue 06: The letter says ninety minutes; the platform says sixty
Original fictional setting: Student Tessa has an approved arrangement specifying 90 minutes for a quiz whose standard duration is 60 minutes. Professor Ali sees that the learning platform still shows the standard setting. A suitable testing-room booking has not been confirmed. They need prompt coordination with the designated access office and testing staff. Tessa is not being asked to disclose a diagnosis to classmates or justify the approved arrangement again.
Professional roles: Tessa / Professor Ali
Published dialogue (reference script, not my own performance):
Tessa: My approved letter specifies ninety minutes for the quiz, but the course platform still shows the standard sixty-minute limit.
Professor Ali: Thank you for flagging it. The implementation detail does not match the approval, and we need to resolve that before relying on the setup.
Tessa: I was worried I would need to explain my diagnosis again to persuade you that the extra time is justified.
Professor Ali: We are discussing the approved accommodation, not asking you to justify it again. Let us focus on the necessary logistics.
Tessa: The testing room was requested last week, but I have not received a booking confirmation from the office.
Professor Ali: Then the testing arrangement is not yet fully confirmed. I will coordinate with the responsible staff rather than assume the request completed the booking.
Tessa: Which office should we include so that the timing setting and room information do not remain in separate conversations?
Professor Ali: I will contact the accessibility office and testing coordinator through the appropriate process, using only the information needed to arrange access.
Tessa: I would prefer not to have my personal situation discussed in a general announcement to the class.
Professor Ali: Of course. We should maintain the confidentiality boundary and use the agreed private channel for your specific arrangements.
Tessa: If the platform limit is changed, can you check what I will actually see rather than only the instructor setting?
Professor Ali: Yes. We need implementation confirmation, including the relevant student-facing view, so an administrative update does not leave the same practical problem.
Tessa: The quiz content itself has not changed, and I understand that the same academic requirements still apply.
Professor Ali: Correct. The essential requirement and the access arrangement are different questions; identical conditions are not the only way to maintain the academic standard.
Tessa: What happens if the requested room cannot be confirmed in time? I do not want to arrive without a workable plan.
Professor Ali: We need a contingency arrangement agreed through the actual process, and I will raise that promptly rather than leave you to improvise.
Tessa: Thank you. A clear confirmation of the duration, location, and contact would resolve the uncertainty for me.
Professor Ali: That is the aim of effective access: the arrangement has to work in practice, not just exist as an approved document.
Tessa: I will use the private channel if the displayed information still conflicts with the confirmation you send.
Professor Ali: Please do. Any remaining access concern needs prompt attention, and I will close the loop when the actual setting and testing arrangements are verified.
Vocabulary in this exchange: approved accommodation: Arrangement approved through the institution's relevant process. / accessibility office: Institutional service coordinating disability-related access arrangements. / implementation detail: Practical setting or action needed to carry out a plan. / testing arrangement: Agreed practical conditions for an assessment. / essential requirement: Core academic or technical requirement under the relevant process. / confidentiality boundary: Limit on sharing personal information.
END REFERENCE

Dialogue 07: A missing source needs a factual explanation
Original fictional setting: A fictional assignment permits AI-assisted brainstorming if disclosed but requires the submitted analysis to be the student's own work. Professor Park cannot locate a cited article and finds that its journal details do not match the supplied reference. Student Amir says he used a tool for an outline and believed the suggested reference was real. No integrity finding or penalty has been determined; the actual institutional review process applies.
Professional roles: Amir / Professor Park
Published dialogue (reference script, not my own performance):
Amir: Your message says there is a concern about my reference list. I am worried that you have already decided I cheated.
Professor Park: No finding has been made. I want to explain a specific citation discrepancy and hear your account through the appropriate process.
Amir: Which reference is the problem? I used a tool to help outline the topic and thought the suggested article was real.
Professor Park: I could not locate that article, and the journal details do not match. It needs source verification rather than an assumption based on a plausible-looking citation.
Amir: The assignment allowed brainstorming, so I understood that I could ask for possible topics and an outline.
Professor Park: It allowed that permitted assistance with disclosure. It also required the submitted analysis to be your own work.
Amir: I included a short note about the outline tool, but I did not explain that the reference came from its suggestion.
Professor Park: We need to examine the actual disclosure statement and the relevant facts, not broaden or narrow the rule during this conversation.
Amir: I understand that even if brainstorming was allowed, I still needed to check whether the cited source existed.
Professor Park: Correct. Accurate attribution and source checking remain important. A convincing format does not establish that a reference is genuine.
Amir: I have the drafts and notes I actually used. Should I keep them as they are rather than try to tidy the history?
Professor Park: Yes. Preserve the relevant process evidence through the appropriate process. Do not create a different history to make the record look cleaner.
Amir: Will this conversation determine the outcome immediately, or is there a separate university procedure I need to understand?
Professor Park: I will explain the applicable route. A concern or allegation is not itself the final determination.
Amir: I want to respond to the specific source issue and understand what information the process asks me to provide.
Professor Park: You should have the stated opportunity to respond, with clear information about the concern and the actual next steps.
Amir: Thank you. I do not want my explanation summarized as admitting things I have not said or that have not been established.
Professor Park: I will record your account accurately and maintain procedural fairness under the institution's process.
Amir: For now, I will preserve the existing materials and respond to the identified question about the source and its use.
Professor Park: That is the next step. Any finding or authorized consequence must be communicated as an actual outcome, not implied in advance by this inquiry.
Vocabulary in this exchange: permitted assistance: Help allowed under the stated assignment rules. / attribution: Identification of the source of ideas, wording, or assistance. / disclosure statement: Account of assistance or tool use required by the task. / source verification: Checking that a cited source exists and supports the use made of it. / citation discrepancy: Mismatch or problem in reference details. / process evidence: Material relevant to how work was developed.
END REFERENCE

Dialogue 07: A missing source needs a factual explanation
Original fictional setting: A fictional assignment permits AI-assisted brainstorming if disclosed but requires the submitted analysis to be the student's own work. Professor Park cannot locate a cited article and finds that its journal details do not match the supplied reference. Student Amir says he used a tool for an outline and believed the suggested reference was real. No integrity finding or penalty has been determined; the actual institutional review process applies.
Professional roles: Amir / Professor Park
Published dialogue (reference script, not my own performance):
Amir: Your message says there is a concern about my reference list. I am worried that you have already decided I cheated.
Professor Park: No finding has been made. I want to explain a specific citation discrepancy and hear your account through the appropriate process.
Amir: Which reference is the problem? I used a tool to help outline the topic and thought the suggested article was real.
Professor Park: I could not locate that article, and the journal details do not match. It needs source verification rather than an assumption based on a plausible-looking citation.
Amir: The assignment allowed brainstorming, so I understood that I could ask for possible topics and an outline.
Professor Park: It allowed that permitted assistance with disclosure. It also required the submitted analysis to be your own work.
Amir: I included a short note about the outline tool, but I did not explain that the reference came from its suggestion.
Professor Park: We need to examine the actual disclosure statement and the relevant facts, not broaden or narrow the rule during this conversation.
Amir: I understand that even if brainstorming was allowed, I still needed to check whether the cited source existed.
Professor Park: Correct. Accurate attribution and source checking remain important. A convincing format does not establish that a reference is genuine.
Amir: I have the drafts and notes I actually used. Should I keep them as they are rather than try to tidy the history?
Professor Park: Yes. Preserve the relevant process evidence through the appropriate process. Do not create a different history to make the record look cleaner.
Amir: Will this conversation determine the outcome immediately, or is there a separate university procedure I need to understand?
Professor Park: I will explain the applicable route. A concern or allegation is not itself the final determination.
Amir: I want to respond to the specific source issue and understand what information the process asks me to provide.
Professor Park: You should have the stated opportunity to respond, with clear information about the concern and the actual next steps.
Amir: Thank you. I do not want my explanation summarized as admitting things I have not said or that have not been established.
Professor Park: I will record your account accurately and maintain procedural fairness under the institution's process.
Amir: For now, I will preserve the existing materials and respond to the identified question about the source and its use.
Professor Park: That is the next step. Any finding or authorized consequence must be communicated as an actual outcome, not implied in advance by this inquiry.
Vocabulary in this exchange: permitted assistance: Help allowed under the stated assignment rules. / attribution: Identification of the source of ideas, wording, or assistance. / disclosure statement: Account of assistance or tool use required by the task. / source verification: Checking that a cited source exists and supports the use made of it. / citation discrepancy: Mismatch or problem in reference details. / process evidence: Material relevant to how work was developed.
END REFERENCE

Dialogue 08: A recommendation is not implementation approval
Original fictional setting: A fictional department committee discusses increasing a seminar enrollment cap from 20 to 30. Professor Grant supports access; Professor Silva asks about feedback workload and room capacity. A motion is amended to recommend a one-term pilot only if staffing and a suitable room are confirmed. The committee votes for that recommendation. Under the supplied local process, a separate faculty board must approve implementation; that approval has not occurred.
Professional roles: Professor Grant / Professor Silva
Published dialogue (reference script, not my own performance):
Professor Grant: I support raising the seminar cap from twenty to thirty. More students want access, and the current limit leaves some out.
Professor Silva: I support that goal too. Before we settle the curriculum proposal, we need to examine the teaching and room assumptions.
Professor Grant: My concern is that resource questions will delay the idea indefinitely, even though the demand is already visible.
Professor Silva: Let us make them specific. The feedback workload increases with enrollment, and the current staffing plan has not addressed that increase.
Professor Grant: We could recommend a limited trial rather than a permanent change, provided the teaching support is confirmed.
Professor Silva: That would be a pilot offering. We should state the duration and conditions clearly instead of leaving them in informal discussion.
Professor Grant: I propose one term, subject to confirmed staffing and a room suitable for thirty participants.
Professor Silva: That is a motion amendment to the original proposal. We need the committee to know exactly which version it is voting on.
Professor Grant: The revised wording still supports increased access, but it does not assume that a larger room and staff already exist.
Professor Silva: Correct. It makes the resource assumption visible and gives the responsible colleagues concrete information to verify.
Professor Grant: Under our department process, does this committee authorize the pilot once the vote is complete?
Professor Silva: No. The faculty board has decision authority for implementation; this committee sends a recommendation under the local process.
Professor Grant: Then the minutes should not say the enrollment increase is approved for next term merely because this vote passes.
Professor Silva: Exactly. The meeting minutes need to record the amended wording and distinguish our recommendation from the board's eventual decision.
Professor Grant: The committee has voted for the amended proposal. I will tell colleagues it is a one-term pilot recommendation with conditions.
Professor Silva: Call it a conditional recommendation, and keep staffing and room confirmation in the same sentence as the proposed increase.
Professor Grant: We can submit the recommendation after identifying the responsible contacts for those checks, without announcing a completed launch.
Professor Silva: Yes. Implementation approval remains pending until the faculty board actually makes that decision.
Professor Grant: If the pilot is approved, we should specify when the department evaluates workload and student participation.
Professor Silva: Include a review checkpoint in the proposal, so a limited trial does not quietly become a permanent change without the appropriate review.
Vocabulary in this exchange: seminar: Academic session centered on discussion and analysis. / curriculum proposal: Suggested change to a program or course structure. / feedback workload: Time and effort required to respond to student work. / resource assumption: Premise about available staffing, space, or support. / motion amendment: Proposed change to the motion under discussion. / meeting minutes: Formal record of discussion and decisions.
END REFERENCE

Lesson 01: Making assignment expectations explicit
Original fictional case: Professor Chen assigns a 600-word comparison of two supplied articles. Students must identify one shared question, explain one difference in the authors' reasoning, and support that comparison with a passage from each article. Outside sources are not required. A formative outline is due Friday; the graded submission is due the following Tuesday. Student Maya has planned two separate summaries.
Language workshop: Compare does not mean summarize twice
Communication goal: Explain the required intellectual task, evidence, and submission details without expanding the assignment.
Language guidance: Two summaries do not necessarily compare reasoning. The supplied task requires a connection between the articles and evidence from both.
Useful expressions (preserve the supplied facts): The goal is to compare their reasoning, not summarize them separately. / Which passage supports the difference you have identified? / Use one passage from each of the two supplied articles. / Outside sources are not required for this assignment. / Friday is the outline; Tuesday is the graded submission. / I will assess how well the evidence supports the comparison. / Tell me which part connects the two authors. / I will post the same clarification for everyone in the course. / Are you asking about the finding or the next step? / Please correct me if I have misunderstood that detail. / That is what the current record says; it has not been independently confirmed. / That is a possibility, not an agreed outcome. / That decision sits outside my authority. / Who is responsible for that specific next step? / Let me restate the distinction more clearly. / We agree on the action, the owner, and the point for review.
Vocabulary: learning outcome: Stated capability students should demonstrate through learning. / assignment brief: Instructions defining a particular assessed or practice task. / comparison: Analysis identifying meaningful similarities or differences. / summary: Condensed account of the main content of a source. / analytical claim: Statement offering an interpretation supported by reasoning and evidence. / textual evidence: Passage or feature of a text supporting an interpretation. / assessment criterion: Standard used to judge a feature of student work. / formative assessment: Practice assessment used to support learning and improvement. / summative assessment: Assessment used to evaluate learning at a defined stage. / submission window: Period during which work can be submitted under stated rules. / word limit: Stated maximum or target length under the task rules. / required reading: Material students are expected to read for the course. / optional resource: Material available but not required for the stated task. / scaffolding: Structured support helping students build toward a task. / prerequisite knowledge: Prior understanding needed for the learning task. / task alignment: Connection between the activity and intended learning. / submission format: Required form or file type for delivering work. / clarification announcement: Shared message resolving an instruction question. / clarification request: Question that resolves an unclear meaning or instruction. / source attribution: Identification of where information came from. / working assumption: Provisional premise used while information is incomplete. / scope boundary: Limit of the work or authority being discussed. / action owner: Named person responsible for a specified next step. / check-back: Restatement used to verify that a message was understood.
Speaking task: Read the corrected exchange and stress compare, support, required, and formative. Swap roles and repeat the three-part task and the two submission stages exactly as supplied. Complete the four-line follow-up with the supplied choices. Check the explanations, then read the corrected exchange twice, changing roles.
Partner: Maya: Student / Professor Chen: Course instructor
Guided response task: Select supplied answers for the dialogue gaps. Check the explanations, then read the completed exchange aloud; no original writing is required.
Optional second-round challenge: A course page labels an additional article optional. The assignment requires only the two supplied core articles. A student assumes the extra article is necessary for credit.
Model for comparison AFTER my attempt, not a response to give me first: Maya: I will organize the outline around that contrast and use the two passages to explain why the distinction matters.
Professor Chen: That matches the learning outcome for this assignment: making a supported comparison rather than recalling each article separately.
Maya: Other students may have read compare the same way I did. Could the course page include this clarification?
Professor Chen: I will post a clarification announcement so everyone has the same instructions, without adding a new requirement or changing the published submission details.
END REFERENCE
